newsitem.title: CHILE: Chileans seen backing Frei in local elections.
newsitem.headline: Chileans seen backing Frei in local elections.

text.p: Chileans will elect their mayors directly for the first time ever on Sunday in nationwide local elections expected to give President Eduardo Frei's centre-left coalition a thumping victory.

Even the government's opponents say the four parties in Frei's coalition, ruling a country with a prosperous economy and stable politics, will win about 50 percent of the vote combined in the elections for mayors and councillors in Chile's 341 cities and towns.
A coalition of two right-wing parties is expected to finish second with about 30 percent, and the rest will be split between smaller parties and independents, opinion polls showed.

"The political balance in Chile won't change very much with these elections,'' said Jovino Novoa, president of the conservative Independent Democratic Union (UDI) party. His party's own polls suggest Frei's coalition will carry about 50 percent of the vote.

But what will change is the way Chileans choose their mayors. Under reforms enacted after the last municipal polls in 1992, Chileans will elect mayors directly for the first time, a change analysts say will benefit politicians with high name recognition like Santiago Mayor Jaime Ravinet.
Under the old system, Chileans elected councillors who then elected the mayor, except during the military regime of 1973-1990 when mayors were appointed by the military.
"People will elect figures with well-known names and personalities. That's the reality," said Ravinet, a member of Frei's Christian Democratic Party.

Known for his red hair and elegant tastes, Ravinet is expected to win reelection easily and could use the results to bolster his reported presidential ambitions in general elections in 1999. He has spent heavily in the campaign despite facing little opposition.
Ravinet's campaign recently published a newspaper ad with endorsements from top Chilean artists and intellectuals, including novelist Antonio Skarmeta and folk singer Isabel Parra.
Also expected to win reelection handily is the mayor of Santiago suburb Las Condes, Joaquin Lavin, an UDI member and nationally prominent figure on the right.

With coalition parties competing separately in the elections, pollsters say two left-wing groups, the Party for Democracy (PPD) and the Socialists, could gain at the expense of the Christian Democrats.

If they do, it will strengthen the position of Public Works Minister Ricardo Lagos, a PPD man, with respect to his Christian Democratic rivals for the coalition's 1999 presidential nomination. Polls show Lagos, well-known as an opponent of military rule in the 1980s, is the only politician in Chile more popular than Frei, who cannot seek reelection.
